questions.q: In unpolarised light from a common source such as the Sun or a lamp, how are the planes of oscillation of the electric field distributed?
options: Only the vertical plane of oscillation is present
Every plane of oscillation perpendicular to the direction of travel is represented
The field oscillates along the direction the light is travelling
The field has no plane of oscillation at all
questions.explanation: Light from a common source (the Sun or a lamp) is unpolarised light, in which every plane of oscillation is represented. The transverse electric field oscillates in all planes perpendicular to the direction of travel, not just one.

questions.q: Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ is passed through a single polarising filter. What is the intensity of the emerging polarised light?
options: Equal to I₀, the intensity is unchanged
One half of I₀, regardless of how the filter is oriented
One quarter of I₀, depending on the angle of the filter
Zero, the filter blocks all of the light
questions.explanation: When unpolarised light passes through a polarising filter, only the component aligned with the filter's axis is passed, so the intensity of the emerging polarised light is half the intensity of the original light: I = ½I₀. This halving happens whatever the filter's orientation.

questions.q: According to Malus's Law, how does the intensity of polarised light emerging from the analyser depend on the angle θ between the axes of the polariser and the analyser?
options: I = I₀ cos θ
I = I₀ cos² θ
I = I₀ sin² θ
I = I₀ / cos² θ
questions.explanation: Malus's Law, discovered by Etienne Malus, gives the intensity of light emerging from the analyser as I = I₀ cos² θ, where I₀ is the maximum intensity of the polarised light falling on the analyser and θ is the angle between the axes of the two filters. The cosine is squared because intensity is proportional to the square of the field amplitude.

questions.q: Why does the observation that light can be polarised show that light is a transverse wave rather than a longitudinal wave?
options: Longitudinal waves travel faster than transverse waves and so escape the filter
Polarisation is a phenomenon that can only occur with transverse waves, because longitudinal waves cannot be polarised
Only longitudinal waves have a plane of oscillation that a filter can restrict
Transverse waves carry no energy through a polarising filter
questions.explanation: A transverse wave has a plane of oscillation perpendicular to the direction of travel, which a polarising filter can restrict to a single plane. Longitudinal waves oscillate along the direction of travel and cannot be polarised, so the polarisation of light shows that light is a transverse wave.

questions.q: From memory: what kind of wave did Huygens originally propose light to be, and how did the discovery of polarisation correct that proposal?
keyPoints: Huygens had proposed that light travelled as longitudinal waves, like sound waves.
Early nineteenth-century physicists became aware of polarisation, a phenomenon that can only occur with transverse waves.
Polarisation therefore showed light is a transverse wave, correcting Huygens on this specific point while keeping the wave model.
questions.explanation: Huygens proposed light was longitudinal like sound, but polarisation is a phenomenon that can only occur with transverse waves, so the discovery that light can be polarised proved light is a transverse wave. Credit Huygens with the wave model, not the transverse nature.

questions.q: Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ passes through a polariser, then through an analyser whose axis is at 60° to the polariser. Find the intensity of the emerging polarised light as a percentage of I₀.
questions.given: Polariser acts on unpolarised light; analyser axis at θ = 60° to the polariser.
questions.explanation: The polariser halves the unpolarised light (no angle), giving 50%. The analyser then applies Malus's Law to the already-polarised light: I = I₀ cos²θ with cos²60° = 0.25, so 0.25 × 50% = 12.5%. This is parts (a) and (b) of Sample Problem 1.

questions.q: Continuing Sample Problem 1, the polarised light emerging at 12.5% of I₀ then falls upon a second analyser whose axis is at 30° to the first analyser. Find the intensity emerging from this third filter as a percentage of I₀.
questions.given: Intensity arriving at the second analyser \(I_b = 0.125\,I_0\); angle between adjacent filters θ = 30°.
working: Malus's Law uses the angle between adjacent filters: θ = 30°
questions.explanation: Use the angle between adjacent filters (30°), not the 90° back to the polariser. I = I₀ cos²θ with cos²30° = 0.75 gives 0.75 × 12.5% ≈ 9.4%. Light gets through even though the first and last filters are crossed at 90°, because the middle analyser re-projects the polarisation — the three-polariser result of part (c).

questions.q: Why can polarising sunglasses, which have a vertical axis, cut through the glare reflected off a horizontal surface such as a pond?
options: The reflected glare is unpolarised, so half of it is always removed
The glare reflected off the horizontal surface is horizontally polarised, and a vertical axis blocks horizontally polarised light
The vertical axis speeds up the light so the glare passes straight through
The sunglasses absorb all light regardless of its plane of polarisation
questions.explanation: Light can be polarised by reflection off hard surfaces such as water. Glare off a horizontal pond is horizontally polarised, so polarising sunglasses with a vertical axis cut through it, but they do not block the vertically polarised glare off a shop window.

questions.q: From memory: when comparing unpolarised and plane-polarised light, which field must you name to earn the marks, and why that field rather than the other?
keyPoints: By convention the plane of polarisation is defined by the electric field, not the magnetic field.

When light interacts with matter (a filter, your eye, a detector) it is overwhelmingly the electric field that pushes the charges around — the electric force dominates the magnetic force at these speeds.
So write: unpolarised light has its electric field oscillating in all planes; plane-polarised light has its electric field oscillating in only one plane.
questions.explanation: The cheapest mark to lose is naming the wrong field. Always say 'electric field' both times in the comparison; the magnetic field is still there and perpendicular, but the plane of polarisation is defined by the electric field because it is the part that interacts with charges.

questions.q: Diffraction, interference and polarisation are the three pillars of evidence for the wave model of light. What makes polarisation unique among the three?
options: It is the only one that proves light is a wave at all
It is the only one of the three that establishes light is specifically a transverse wave
It is the only one that works for sound as well as light
It is the only one that can be demonstrated without a filter
questions.explanation: Diffraction and interference both prove light is a wave, but sound (a longitudinal wave) also diffracts and interferes, so they cannot settle the transverse question. Only polarisation shows light is specifically a transverse wave — the deep end of 'DIP into the wave model'.
